rationale: A wins because it keeps four genuinely separate editorial doors open and does not turn its biggest proof gaps into claims. Its "Skydio says its power-line drones fly with no pilot at all — regulators will want specifics" is a real beat angle that B wrongly bins as "hallucinated_fact." B's "A US drone maker bets the grid will pay a premium to avoid Chinese hardware" invents buyer price behavior the update never gave it, which is how a decent angle becomes a liability.
gaps_in_A: "Power-line and substation inspection is dangerous, manual, and expensive work utilities have wanted to automate for years" is plausible trade context, but it is not in the supplied update and needs sourcing.

"the first major public proof point since the consumer exit" overclaims. The update says Skydio exited consumer drones two years ago and is launching this drone now; it does not say this is first, major, live, or the proof point.
"wildfire-risk mitigation" may be relevant to power-line inspection, but the update never mentions wildfire risk. That beat needs evidence before it belongs in the angle.
"None of these four angles has a fatal hole" is too generous. The lack of a named utility is a serious pitch handicap, especially for the operations and pivot stories.
gaps_in_B: "will pay a premium to avoid Chinese hardware" is invented. The update says US-made positioning against Chinese makers facing import restrictions; it says nothing about a premium or buyer willingness to pay one.
"no named utility willing to say so" imputes unwillingness. The release discloses no named utility; that is all the facts support.

"The safety case: what happens when an unpiloted drone fails over a live substation" gets refused as "hallucinated_fact," but the safety/regulatory question is a valid angle if framed around authorization and failsafes rather than an imagined failure.
"what the drone industry decided its actual business was" is too grand from one company update. One Skydio pivot does not prove an industry conclusion.
